title: continuous-batching-scheduler-tuning-experiments-6
content:
Objective:
Run systematic tuning of the continuous batching scheduler to understand tradeoffs between batch size caps, max wait timeout, and fairness policies on tail latency and throughput. Goal is to produce recommended defaults and a short decision tree for workload types (low-latency interactive vs high-throughput batch).

Background / Motivation:
- Continuous batching reduces per-token cost by combining in-flight requests, but misconfigured batching can significantly hurt tail latency for interactive workloads.
- Historically we used a conservative default: max_batch_size=16, max_delay_ms=25, fairness=fifo. Customer reports and internal benchmarks show p99 spikes for small request rates and heterogeneous request sizes.
- Need empirical guidance and a small autosuggest rule-set for Redwood Optimize and Dedicated configs.

High-level hypotheses:
1) Increasing max_batch_size raises throughput and lowers average cost/tk but increases p99, especially at low QPS due to head-of-line blocking.
2) Higher max_delay_ms increases batching opportunity and throughput, but increases median and tail latency; adaptive timeouts can get most throughput benefit with lower tail impact.
3) Fairness policies that prioritize small requests or use size-aware merging can reduce p99 for short requests without losing much throughput.
4) A hybrid profile (small_timeout + adaptive bump when queueing >N) will give best tail/throughput balance for mixed workloads.

Experimental matrix:
- Batch size caps tested: [4, 8, 16, 32]
- Max delay (ms) tested: [5, 10, 25, 50]
- Fairness modes: [fifo, size-aware-priority, age-priority, adaptive-timeout]
- Workload shapes: [steady-high-qps (200 req/s), steady-low-qps (5 req/s), bursty (10s bursts at 400 req/s), mixed-size (50% short ~2 tokens, 50% long ~80 tokens)]
- Model: rwd-7b-quant (representative open model used on Dedicated clusters)
- Hardware: single A100 40GB GPU per worker; runtime version 2.17.1; CUDA 12.1; cuDNN 9.5

Metrics captured:
- p50/p95/p99 tail latencies (ms) measured end-to-end (request arrive -> first token out)
- throughput (requests/sec) and tokens/sec
- batching efficiency: avg batch occupancy (tokens aggregated / max_tokens_possible) and avg batch size (requests)
- cost proxy: GPU utilization and tokens/sec per GPU
- fairness indicators: distribution of latency by request size class

Methodology:
- Warm-up 5 minutes per config, measure for next 10 minutes, repeat 3 runs, report median of runs.
- Synthetic clients emulate arrival patterns with realistic client-side think time and request size distribution.
- Disable KV caching to isolate scheduling effects for these runs.
- Use logging and flamegraph profiling for scheduler hot paths to ensure no CPU-side bottlenecks were introduced by fairness logic.

Key results summary (high-level):
- Throughput and cost:
  - Increasing max_batch_size from 8 -> 32 increased tokens/sec per GPU by ~18-25% under high qps steady workload.
  - Larger batches reached higher GPU utilization, reducing estimated cost/tk proportionally.

- Latency (median vs tail):
  - p50 moved modestly with batching (p50 improved slightly for large batches because GPU utilization reduced per-token service time), e.g., p50 35ms @ batch=8 -> 30ms @ batch=32 on steady-high-qps.
  - p95 increased significantly with larger batch_size and larger delay. Example: p95 ~90ms @ (batch=8, delay=10ms) -> ~170ms @ (batch=32, delay=50ms) on mixed-size workload.
  - p99 showed the largest sensitivity: for low-qps steady workload p99 jumped from ~120ms @ (batch=8, delay=10ms) to ~700ms @ (batch=32, delay=50ms).

- Fairness policies:
  - size-aware-priority reduced p99 for short requests by ~40-60% compared to fifo at same batch/delay settings, with <5% throughput loss in most configs.
  - age-priority prevents starvation of long-waiting requests but sometimes reduced batching efficiency modestly.
  - adaptive-timeout (start with 5ms, escalate to 25ms if queue >6) captured most throughput gains of high max_delay while keeping p99 within 20% of low-delay configs.

- Adaptive timeout vs fixed delay:
  - Best overall tradeoff: max_batch_size=16, adaptive-timeout policy (base=5ms, escalate thresholds at queue lengths 6/12), results: p50 ~32ms, p95 ~95ms, p99 ~180ms, throughput ~85% of max achievable at batch=32/fixed-50ms.
  - Pure fixed high delay (50ms) gave slightly higher throughput but p99 often >3x of adaptive config, making it unacceptable for interactive SLAs.

- CPU/Runtime overhead:
  - Size-aware and adaptive policies added ~2-4% CPU scheduling overhead (measured in scheduler thread), no noticeable GPU stalls. Flamegraphs show added branching in scheduler path but not hot enough to warrant optimization now.

Representative numbers (mixed-size workload, median run):
- Config A (batch=8, delay=10ms, fifo): p50=34ms, p95=92ms, p99=125ms, throughput=750 req/s, avg_batch_size=6.2
- Config B (batch=32, delay=50ms, fifo): p50=30ms, p95=170ms, p99=690ms, throughput=930 req/s, avg_batch_size=20.9
- Config C (batch=16, adaptive-timeout, size-aware): p50=32ms, p95=95ms, p99=180ms, throughput=840 req/s, avg_batch_size=12.7

Observations & interpretation:
- The largest contributor to p99 is queuing delay waiting for batches to fill; this is especially visible at low request rates where the scheduler holds a short request to fill a batch and long-tail suffers.
- Size-aware fairness prevents small requests from being stuck behind long ones in a batch by preferentially forming micro-batches, which reduces p99 for interactive cases while preserving most batching gains.
- Adaptive timeouts give most benefits by allowing fast dispatch when queue is small and more aggressive batching when backlog warrants it.
- Purely increasing max_batch_size is a blunt instrument: it improves throughput but at the cost of unacceptable tail latency for many customer SLAs.

Recommendations (practical defaults):
1) Default scheduler profile for hosted API (interactive-first):
   - max_batch_size: 16
   - base_max_delay_ms: 5ms
   - adaptive-timeout: escalate to 25ms when queue length > 6, further escalate to 50ms when queue > 16 (to support burst absorption)
   - fairness: size-aware-priority enabled
   Rationale: Good balance of throughput and p99; handles bursts without degrading steady interactive latency.

2) Default for high-throughput/Dedicated reserved workloads (throughput-first):
   - max_batch_size: 32
   - max_delay_ms: 50ms
   - fairness: fifo (unless user opts-in for size-aware)
   - Provide an option to enable size-aware to protect short requests if workload is mixed.

3) Autosuggest rules in Redwood Optimize / console:
   - If observed p99 > SLA and avg queue length < 4 -> lower base_max_delay_ms or enable size-aware.
   - If GPU utilization < 60% and p95/p99 within SLA -> suggest increasing max_batch_size or max_delay.
   - If workload has >30% short requests -> suggest enabling size-aware fairness.

Action items / next steps:
- Ship a beta scheduler profile in next runtime release (2.18.x): interactive-default (config 1) and throughput-default (config 2). Owner: Mark Chen. ETA: 3 weeks.
- Add telemetry hooks to Console: per-route avg_batch_size, p99 broken down by request-size quantiles, and adaptive-timeout triggers. Owner: Sofia Martinez. ETA: 4 weeks.
- Run a 24h customer-facing A/B test on Dedicated clusters with default=old and new interactive-default to validate real-world impact. Owner: Solutions Eng lead. ETA: Q2 pilot.
- Follow-up micro-optimizations: reduce scheduler branching cost for size-aware logic if CPU overhead >5% on smaller instances. Owner: Liam O'Connor. ETA: next sprint.

Notes / open questions:
- Need to validate behavior with KV caching and longer-context models; caching can change request service time footprint and batching dynamics.
- Evaluate interactions with multi-tenant preemption and per-customer quotas - adaptive-timeout thresholds may need per-tenant tuning.
- Consider exposing a lightweight simulator in Optimize to let customers approximate their expected p99 given sample traffic traces and proposed scheduler settings.
